newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thyssen profits seen down, to restructure.
newsitem.headline: Thyssen profits seen down, to restructure.

text.p: German steel and engineering group Thyssen AG is expected to announce a big drop in profits when it publishes 1995-96 results on Friday, steel industry analysts said on Wednesday.
Thyssen's supervisory board will also discuss plans to sell off loss-making units and build on core areas to boost returns and increase its emphasis on shareholder value.

Richard Schramm, analyst at Trinkaus Capital Management, said he saw pre-tax profits falling to 700 million marks ($466.3 million) in the year to end-September from 1.026 billion. Net profits are likely to fall to 480 million from 749 million.
Analysts said that, with sales likely to decline slightly from the previous year's 39 billion marks, Thyssen needed to revolutionise its business to slim down and increase margins.
"This is an industry which needs less capacity and higher returns," said Alan Coats at Merrill Lynch in London. "Thyssen has got to decide what it's core strengths are."
Details of the group's restructuring strategy have appeared in the German press this week, encouraging investors to drive up the Thyssen share price 14 marks to 283.50 on Wednesday.

But analysts said the reports, dismissed as "speculation" by Thyssen's Duesseldorf headquarters, were not new. Chief executive Dieter Vogel had briefed them on his strategy at the publication of half-year results last summer.
"This is absolutely nothing new," Schramm said. Analysts said Vogel had told them the restructuring would be finalised by September, but had heard nothing since.
Thyssen's share rally was driven by magazine and newspaper reports that Vogel was seeking to raise returns on capital to 12.5 percent throughout the Thyssen group.

To achieve that, subsidiaries with five billion marks in turnover would have to be sold off within a year in a bid to erase losses of 300 million marks per year, the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said, quoting industry sources.
Divisions to go would include armaments, while the sale of Thyssen's long steel operations to Georgsmarienhuette GmbH is already under way.

Analysts said that Thyssen -- which failed in its bid to buy a stake in DBKom, the telecommunications unit of Deutsche Bahn state railways -- may sell out its stake in the E+ German mobile phone network to its partner Veba AG.

That would leave the group free to concentrate on its core businesses of flat steel -- with capacity of eight million tonnes per year. It would also seek to build its car parts, materials trading, elevator and machine-building businesses.

Earnings per share figures are not likely to be published until the release of Thyssen's final results, but analysts see the 1995-96 figure at between 13 and 16 marks, down from 24 marks. Next year's EPS is seen at 20-21 marks. -- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150 ($1=1.5011 Mark)
